name: Valera and Queries
description: Valera loves segments. He has recently come up with one interesting problem. The Ox axis of coordinates has n segments, the i -th segment starts in position l i and ends in position r i (we will mark it as [ l i , r i ] ). Your task is to process m queries, each consists of number cnt i and a set of cnt i coordinates of points located on the Ox axis. The answer to the query is the number of segments, such that each of them contains at least one point from the query. Segment [ l , r ] contains point q , if l ≤ q ≤ r . Valera found the solution of this problem too difficult. So he asked you to help him. Help Valera.
input_specification: The first line contains two integers n , m ( 1 ≤ n , m ≤ 3·10 5 ) — the number of segments on the axis of coordinates and the number of queries. Next n lines contain the descriptions of the segments. The i -th line contains two positive integers l i , r i ( 1 ≤ l i ≤ r i ≤ 10 6 ) — the borders of the i -th segment. Next m lines contain the description of the queries, one per line. Each line starts from integer cnt i ( 1 ≤ cnt i ≤ 3·10 5 ) — the number of points in the i -th query. Then the line contains cnt i distinct positive integers p 1 , p 2 , ..., p cnt i ( 1 ≤ p 1 < p 2 < ... < p cnt i ≤ 10 6 ) — the coordinates of points in the i -th query. It is guaranteed that the total number of points in all queries doesn't exceed 3·10 5 .
output_specification: Print m non-negative integers, where the i -th number is the response to the i -th query.
approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 369E — Valera and Queries [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
